title: How to help someone with opioid addiction: 10 ways to support their treatment
summary: Learn how to help someone with opioid addiction, from supporting their treatment and medication to what to do if your loved one isn’t ready for help yet.
body_markdown:
Opioid use disorder (OUD) is a chronic medical condition, and treating it is a long-term process that often takes a toll on the well-being of family members. If you’re trying to figure out how to help someone with addiction, know that you have more influence than it might feel like right now. Support from family can make it more likely that a loved one starts treatment and stays in it. For practical advice, we asked Adam Bisaga, MD, Ophelia’s Senior Medical Director, to share tips from his book, *Overcoming Opioid Addiction* . Below are 10 ways to support someone in treatment, plus what to do if they aren’t ready to start yet.


## 1. Remember that opioid use disorder is a medical condition


While it may be easy to fall into the trap of perceiving addiction as selfish or as a “choice,” when you compare opioid use disorder against other chronic disorders like diabetes or heart disease, the concept isn’t much different — and it’s important to remember that as your loved one begins treatment.


Believing that addiction is a disorder rather than a voluntary choice sometimes requires a leap of faith. Because people who use opioids can remain rational in most other areas of their lives, it seems that their behavior around drugs is knowing and deliberate. With that, most families reject the reasoning that drug use has become involuntary and compulsive. They become angry rather than compassionate, accusatory rather than supportive. They initially reject the comparison to other medical disorders as well. Only over time do they begin to accept it, which becomes a relief for many families. But the evidence does not lie. Brain-imaging studies that evaluated the activity of areas of the brain involved in maintaining uncontrollable drug use show changes in function as compared to otherwise healthy brains. Thankfully, those brain changes resolve after a period of abstinence, which means that the brain can heal, damage is not permanent, and people can return to full health.


The words you use matter, too. Saying “a person with OUD” instead of “an addict” sounds like a small change, but it can make it easier for your loved one to talk to you honestly and to ask for help when they need it.


## 2. Understand the difference between outpatient + residential treatment for opioid addiction


Residential programs have long been considered the gold standard when it comes to addiction treatment options. But they may not necessarily be better for a person with OUD, as people with OUD primarily need medical treatment. While they offer their residents a lot in terms of services and support for mental health, it is difficult to predict who will benefit from residential versus outpatient treatment. When treating OUD with medications, which requires long-term follow-up, outpatient treatment usually makes more sense financially and logistically.


Outpatient care now includes telehealth, too. With[online opioid addiction treatment](https://ophelia.com/treatment-online-opioid-addiction-treatment) , your loved one can meet with a clinician by video and, when it’s clinically appropriate, pick up their prescription at a local pharmacy without stepping away from work or family. Residential or inpatient care may still be the better fit for someone with severe medical or psychiatric needs or an unsafe living situation. Whichever setting you look at, make sure the program offers, or at least allows, FDA-approved medication for OUD.


## 3. Know what questions to ask treatment providers


These questions can help you and your loved one compare programs before committing to one:


- Do you prohibit the use of any medications? If yes, which medications?
- How long is the program?
- Is there a wait list?
- What does treatment cost?
- What are average out-of-pocket expenses after insurance?
- How do you help families use their health insurance to pay for treatment?
- What percentage of people are discharged on medications?
- What treatment do people usually go to after discharge? And how do you make sure they connect with that program?
- Do you follow up with the people after they leave the program?
- Is there an option to follow up with the primary therapist on the phone after discharge? Is it a scheduled or “as-needed” follow-up?
- What happens if a person struggles and wants to come back to treatment?


Be cautious of any program that guarantees results or won’t discuss medication.


## 4. Know that your loved one’s treatment isn’t your full responsibility, but you do play a large role


In early treatment, people need a lot of support, more than you might think necessary. Thinking and concentration can be foggy for a while, as the brain adjusts. Energy is low because a good night’s sleep is hard to come by, at least initially. A car, job, or money might be issues. Basic skills, from hygiene to job interviewing, might be lacking. All of this is because of a serious chronic illness. If your loved one suffered from a serious disorder other than addiction, how would you treat them? Would you help them learn to do new things? Drive them to appointments? Support them financially? Make sure they take their medication and stay in touch with their care team? Help them apply for a job?


If your loved one is in online addiction treatment, “driving them to appointments” might look like making sure they have a charged phone and a quiet, private spot for video visits. And supporting them doesn’t mean absorbing every consequence of their opioid use. If you’re not sure where to draw the line, our guide to[setting boundaries with a loved one using opioids](https://ophelia.com/blog/8-ways-to-set-boundaries-with-a-loved-one-using-opioids-without-cutting-them-off) can help.


## 5. Consider medication-assisted treatment (MAT)


Without medication, the risk of returning to opioid use after detox or rehab is high. In one follow-up study of people discharged from inpatient opioid detox,[91% returned to opioid use](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20669601/) , and more than half did so within the first week. (1) That’s where medical interventions come into play for someone with (OUD). With a nFDA-approved medication prescribed by a clinician, your friend or family member can stop using heroin or fentanyl or misusing prescription opioids while easing withdrawal symptoms, (2) relieving cravings, (2) lowering the chances of relapse, (2) and reducing the risk of overdose. In a study of more than 40,000 people with OUD, treatment with buprenorphine or methadone was linked to a 76% lower risk of overdose at three months and a 59% lower risk at 12 months. (3) To learn more about this effective treatment plan (that’s an alternative to traditional 12-step programs), refer to our[full guide on how to help someone struggling with opioids without rehab](https://ophelia.com/blog/how-to-help-addict-without-rehab) .


Medication works best alongside ongoing support from a care team, and for many people it’s a long-term treatment, the same way medication is for other chronic conditions. If your loved one wants to compare options, our overview of[FDA-approved medications for opioid use disorder](https://ophelia.com/blog/suboxone-r-alternatives-other-fda-approved-medications-for-opioid-use-disorder-oud) walks through each one


## 6. **Help them stay on their medication**


[Between 50% and 80% of people](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31786933/) who start[buprenorphine](https://ophelia.com/blog/what-is-buprenorphine) stop taking it within several weeks or months (4) , and some do so because they feel they are back to “normal.” Many people question whether they need to keep taking it, especially when they feel so good. Yet they still have a chronic disorder, their brain is slowly healing, and they are exposed to stress and cravings, which leave them vulnerable to a return to use. Stopping medication too soon can raise the risk of overdose, so any change should be a decision your loved one makes with their clinician. Here’s how you can help support them.


- Be present when the medication is picked up from the pharmacy
- Help keep medication in a safe place that’s locked and out of reach of children and pets, since buprenorphine can be life-threatening if a child takes it
- Dispense it at scheduled times
- Supervise when medication is taken
- Accompany your loved ones for naltrexone or buprenorphine injections like Sublocade
- Set clear expectations for taking medications in return for your support
- Clearly communicate benefits and rewards for taking medication and consequences for not taking it


## 7. Accept ambivalence as part of treatment


Ambivalence is normal. People with OUD are exposed to a lot of stressors and triggers which cause them to want to use. Sometimes your loved one will be motivated to stay on track; other days they will feel conflicted and may fall back into old patterns. Once you expect and accept this, you will find the seesaw characteristics of ambivalence much easier to deal with. Here’s how you can help:


- Ask questions about why your loved one is feeling unsure
- Ask about their reasons for change and their belief in the ability to change
- Emphasize their strengths, all the positive actions they have already taken
- Acknowledge that early can be difficult


If your loved one does return to use, try not to treat it as failure. With any chronic condition, a setback is a sign that the treatment plan may need adjusting. The most helpful thing you can do is encourage them to tell their care team as soon as possible.


## 8. **Put household expectations in writing**


A family agreement is a written “contract” you can use to reward behaviors that are good for treatment and discourage behaviors that are not. It borrows from contingency management, an evidence-based approach that uses rewards to reinforce positive changes. It sets clear expectations and limits so everyone in the household knows what is expected of them. Lead with what you want to see more of, like showing up to appointments or taking medication as prescribed, rather than with punishments.


## 9. Have everyone in the household review their relationship with drugs and put use on hold


Drinking or smoking weed in front of the person in early treatment is a trigger. Having opioid pain medication around is detrimental. In time, your loved one may not see alcohol as a trigger, but in the beginning they may. Here’s how you can help:


- Remove all drug paraphernalia from the home
- Remove all alcohol and other drugs from the home
- If you are prescribed opioid pain medication, lock it up and do not take it in front of your loved one
- Avoid using all other drugs, including alcohol, in front of your loved one; set a new normal — a drug-free home
- Keep naloxone (Narcan) somewhere easy to find and[learn how to use it](https://ophelia.com/blog/how-to-administer-naloxone) , since it can reverse an opioid overdose and is available without a prescription


## 10. Get help for yourself


Addiction’s toll on a family gets worse before it can get better. Even when a loved one is making progress in treatment, family members need help. Don’t underestimate how important self-care is for you and other family members. Reach out to others for support. Find a counselor, attend a family support group, or attend Al-Anon or Nar-Anon meetings. SMART Recovery Family & Friends offers a science-based alternative, and a therapist trained in CRAFT (Community Reinforcement and Family Training) can teach you specific skills for supporting your loved one. If you are struggling to cope, a therapist of your own can help you and can also help you find ways to keep the conversation with your loved one open.


## **What if your loved one isn’t ready for treatment?**


Many families are told to wait until their loved one hits “rock bottom.” You don’t have to wait. Treatment doesn’t need to be voluntary to be effective (5), and with[fentanyl in the drug supply](https://ophelia.com/fentanyl-addiction-treatment) , every stretch of opioid use carries a real risk of overdose.


One of the best-studied approaches for families is CRAFT. Instead of confrontation, it teaches you to reward the time your loved one spends not using, step back from shielding them from the consequences of use, and look for moments when they’re more open to talking. In a review of studies, CRAFT helped about two-thirds of people who were refusing treatment to start it. It was about three times more effective than Al-Anon or Nar-Anon facilitation and about twice as effective as a confrontational intervention. (6)


When you do talk about treatment, a few things tend to help:


- Pick a calm moment when your loved one isn’t high or in withdrawal.
- Describe what you’ve noticed and how it makes you feel, instead of using labels or accusations.
- Listen more than you talk, and ask what they want for their own life.
- Have treatment information ready, so if they say yes, the next step is easy.
- Let them know the door stays open, even if the answer today is no.


If you ever think your loved one is overdosing, call 911 and give naloxone right away. Our[opioid overdose response guide](https://ophelia.com/blog/what-to-do-if-someone-is-overdosing) covers the warning signs.


## **How Ophelia supports people in treatment**


Ophelia provides online treatment for opioid use disorder, currently[available in a handful of states](https://ophelia.com/local-help) . Each patient works with a dedicated[care team](https://ophelia.com/meet) made up of a prescribing clinician, a nurse, and a care coordinator, through private video visits from home. When it’s clinically appropriate, clinicians prescribe medication like[Suboxone](https://ophelia.com/suboxone-doctors) , sent to a local pharmacy, and support is available seven days a week.


Ophelia accepts many insurance plans, including Medicaid and Medicare, and many patients pay less than $10/month for care. See[insurance and pricing](https://ophelia.com/insurance-and-pricing) for details. If your loved one is open to it, they can[check their insurance coverage](https://my.ophelia.com/insurance-coverage) online or[schedule a welcome call](https://welcome.ophelia.com/welcome) to ask questions before getting started.


## **Frequently asked questions**


### **How can I help someone with opioid addiction who doesn’t want help?**


Stay connected and keep conversations calm and free of blame. Approaches like CRAFT teach families to reward time spent not using, let natural consequences happen, and bring up treatment when their loved one seems most open to it. Keep naloxone on hand, and make it clear you’ll help them get started whenever they’re ready.


### **Should I let my loved one hit rock bottom?**


No. Waiting for rock bottom isn’t necessary for treatment to work, and with fentanyl in the drug supply, waiting can be deadly. Treatment can be effective even when someone starts out unsure. Encouraging treatment early, while setting firm boundaries around money and behavior, is safer than pulling your support away completely.


### **What should I say to someone in treatment for opioid addiction?**


Keep it simple and honest. Let them know you’re proud of them and that you’re there, without turning every conversation into a check-in about their treatment. Ask how they’re doing and listen more than you talk. Avoid labels, lectures, and “just stay strong” clichés. On hard days, “I’m here, and I’m not going anywhere” often helps more than advice.


### **Is taking Suboxone just trading one addiction for another?**


No.[Buprenorphine](https://ophelia.com/buprenorphine-treatment) , the main medication in Suboxone, is FDA-approved to treat opioid use disorder. It eases withdrawal and cravings and lowers overdose risk. Taking a prescribed medication as directed, even daily and long-term, isn’t the same as addiction, which involves compulsive use despite harm.


### **How can I help a family member with opioid addiction?**


Start by learning how the condition works and keeping the conversation open and free of blame. Encourage FDA-approved medication and treatment, help with practical things like appointments and refills, set clear boundaries around money, and keep naloxone at home. Supporting a family member also means supporting yourself, so lean on groups like Al-Anon or Nar-Anon.


### **What should I do if my loved one relapses?**


Stay calm and avoid shaming them. A return to use is common with a chronic condition and usually means the treatment plan needs adjusting. Encourage them to contact their care team right away, keep naloxone nearby, and remind them that one setback doesn’t erase the progress they’ve made.


### **Can I be involved in my loved one’s treatment?**


Yes, with their permission. Federal privacy rules protect substance use treatment records, so clinicians generally need your loved one’s written consent before sharing details of their care with you. You can still help in practical ways, like keeping track of appointments, helping with refills, and making room for private telehealth visits.


### **Does insurance cover opioid addiction treatment?**


Many insurance plans, including Medicaid and Medicare, cover medication for opioid use disorder. With Ophelia, many patients with accepted insurance or medicaid plans pay less than $10/month. Your loved one can check their coverage online in a few minutes.
